newsitem.title: UK: Emerging currencies supplant Europe high yielders.
newsitem.headline: Emerging currencies supplant Europe high yielders.

text.p: Emerging market currencies like the Czech crown, South African rand and Philippine peso will continue to play a key role in the international bond market as a source of substantial yield, dealers said on Thursday.

Last year the Portuguese escudo, Spanish peseta and Italian lira were considered high yielding currencies, but European Economic and Monetary Union convergence has meant yield pick-up is not as enticing and investors are looking around for more.

"Emerging market currencies are the bread, butter and jam for investors seeking higher returns for their dough," a dealer at a U.S. bank in London said. "The current supply is a continuation of their hunger for yield," he added.

Fresh currency sectors are expected to see more activity to appease investors hungry for yield. The Eastern European currencies -- Slovak crown, Hungarian forint and Polish zloty -- are expected to become the next area of exploration and from Asia, issuance is expected in Korean won.
Czech crown and rand supply accounted for more than $3.0 billion equivalent in the first quarter this year, 76 transactions in total, Capital DATA Bondware showed.
Retail investors in Austria, Benelux, Germany, Italy and Switzerland are the key recipients of the paper.

"There will be continuing issuance in Czech crowns and rand," a trader at a European bank said. "Spain and Italy are not offering enough yield. The emerging currencies attract investors that used to buy lira and pesetas."

AAA-rated supranationals have taken the lead in raising money in emerging currencies as the combination of a top-notch credit and currency exposure works well, traders said. Investors are prepared to take the currency risk for such high returns because of the lower degree of credit risk.

European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, European Investment Bank, Inter-American Development Bank, International Finance Corp and World Bank are loyal borrowers in emerging market currencies.
Czech crowns and rand have up until now competed for attention while the recent opening up of the Philippine peso market has added another dimension.

"Investors are bullish on the rand after the (South African) budget, and the Czech crown is a good proxy for the mark. The Philippines is also the best improving credit story in Asia," an emerging market syndicate manager at a U.S. bank said.

The positive South African yield curve means maturities can extend to the recent 30-year duration seen on zero coupon bonds. The inverse Czech crown yield curve means issues are confined to the short end.

"The pace of rand supply has superseded the Czech crown Eurobond supply. It was the knock-on effect from all the zero coupon rand bonds sold to institutional investors which have given the sector a fillip," the syndicate manager added.
European banks like Commerzbank and Deutsche Bank and well-regarded corporates like Nestle and Volkswagen have also been keen borrowers in emerging currencies.

For borrowers, the attraction lies in favourable swap rates from the emerging currencies into dollars which enables funding at sub-LIBOR rates. Issuers also gain name-recognition in fledgling sectors.

"Attractive funding levels, publicity for innovative structures like the recent zero coupon rand bonds and the potential to tap a broader investor base are all enticing issuers," a syndicate official at a Canadian bank said.
"There's always a lot in the pipeline, if demand continues the way we are seeing it right now, then we'll see a lot more as it captures the imagination."
